By Friday, you can see through the barista. Not a little. You can read the menu through his chest. He's been making your coffee for two years. You've never asked his name.
And he's not the only one.
It starts on Monday. The man in the lift is a bit pale. You assume it's the lighting.
On Tuesday, Dana is talking to you while you answer an email. Halfway through her sentence, you notice you can see the printer behind her.
…so that's my news. What do you think?
She fades a little more. You watch it happen.
Dana. Sorry. I wasn't listening. Tell me about your cat.

She tells you. The cat was called Biscuit, and he hated everyone except her. With every sentence, she gets a little more solid. So that's the rule. Ignore someone, and they fade. Pay attention, and they come back.
You get good at it. You learn the barista's name: Kofi. You ask the lift man about his dog. You stop typing when your boss talks, which surprises him more than anyone.
Nobody listens. This is very unsettling.
By Thursday, the city looks solid again. You're exhausted. Paying attention, it turns out, is a full-time job.
On Friday night, you get home, drop onto the sofa, and open your phone.
I said, did you see the—
You can see the cushions through your brother. Not a little. Almost all the way.
You checked everyone. The barista, the lift, the boss. You never checked the person on your sofa.
He tells you. All of it. The match, the referee, a goal he's still angry about. Then, somehow, his job interview on Monday, which you didn't know about.
Tell me a third time. I'm listening now.
By midnight, he's solid again. Fully, annoyingly solid. He's eaten all your crisps.
Kofi looks so surprised you think he might drop the cup. He doesn't fade. Neither does anyone else. Not this week.
Who would be fading around you right now?
